cases.description: A full RFC 3339 UTC date-time with millisecond precision is accepted and parses to whole milliseconds.
A date-time with a numeric +HH:MM offset is accepted and normalized to the same instant.
A date-time without fractional seconds is accepted.
Sub-millisecond precision is truncated to whole milliseconds, so an implementation comparing at nanoseconds would diverge here.
February 29 in a leap year is a valid date and is accepted.
A four-digit year below 0100 is the literal year, so an implementation that mapped 0..99 to 1900..1999 would diverge here.
A pre-epoch instant with sub-millisecond precision floors to the containing millisecond (negative), so a truncate-toward-zero implementation would diverge.
February 29 in a non-leap year is out of range and is rejected; a parser that normalizes it to March 1 would diverge.
A day past the end of the month (June 31) is rejected rather than rolled into the next month.
Hour 24 is out of range and is rejected rather than rolled into the next day.
A comma fractional-second separator is rejected; the grammar requires a dot, even though some parsers accept a comma.
A date with no time component is not a full RFC 3339 date-time and is rejected.
A date-time without a zone designator is rejected; the instant would be ambiguous.
A space instead of the RFC 3339 `T` separator is rejected even though some lenient parsers accept it.
A lowercase `t` separator is rejected; the grammar requires an uppercase `T`.
A syntactically shaped but out-of-range date (month 13) is rejected.
An empty string is not a timestamp.
Second 60 (a leap second) is out of the accepted 00..59 range and is rejected, even though it is a value UTC itself sometimes has.
A lowercase `z` zone designator is rejected; the grammar requires an uppercase `Z`.
A numeric offset with an hour field of 25 is out of the 00..23 range and is rejected.
A numeric offset with a minute field of 70 is out of the 00..59 range and is rejected.
A -00:00 offset is accepted and is equal to Z, the same instant as the zone-designator form.
A +00:00 offset is accepted and is the same instant as -00:00 and Z.
A timestamp padded with trailing fractional-second zero digits to exactly the 64-character length cap is accepted; only the millisecond digits are significant.
One character past the 64-character length cap is rejected before parsing, even though the value would otherwise be a well-formed timestamp.
